speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addition to the comments I am about to make regarding this particular amendment, including various reasons why I feel the amendment is redundant, I should also like to take this opportunity to explain the government's general position with respect to amendments that are presented to the House at this stage, undoubtedly for perfectly good reasons, with a view to further improving the charter. Of course there is room for improvement in the charter like everything else that is made by man, and we admit as much. However, 1 would like to suggest to the House that at this stage, any further amendment such as the one presented by the hon. member opposite and the one that has just been defeated and which was moved by the member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), is actually a threat to the accord concluded on November 5 which finally gave us our own constitution amendable in Canada with a charter of rights, of which a member of the opposition has just said that it was very good in its present form.
I shall first address the substance of the amendment. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has explained several times in this House, in point and verbally on other occasions, that in his view, which is supported by his own Department of Justice, the charter is at this point in time neutral with respect to abortion. In other words, the charter does not say whether abortions will be easier or more difficult to practise in the future. The charter is absolutely neutral on this matter, and according to the interpretation of senior officials and agents of the Department of Justice and according to the minister himself, under the constitution the House retains the right to amend the Criminal Code, which is the statute affecting the issue of abortion. So, as I said yesterday, I believe, in answer to a question by the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), the House will probably have to decide in the weeks, months or years ahead, depending on the wishes of its members, whether the Criminal Code should be amended to make abortion less readily or more readily available. The onus will be on us. This, Mr. Speaker, is to reassure those who feel that under the charter we are losing some of our rights with respect to abortion. However, as I said yesterday to the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, should a judge conclude that on the contrary, the charter does, to a certain extent, affect certain provisions of the Criminal Code, under the override clause we reserve the right to say: Notwithstanding this decision, notwithstanding the charter of rights as interpreted by this judge, the House legislates in such and such a manner on the abortion issue.
Mr. Speaker, that is our general argument. Moreover, towards the end of his speech I heard the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) say that there were still people who had some doubts about this, and he said, and I hope I am quoting him correctly:

"We want the doubters to come home. "We want the doubters to feel reassured as a result of this charter, and, therefore, I am proposing an amendment relating to abortion".
Once again I think what the hon. member is doing is being done with the utmost of good faith. But I wonder why he does not also attempt to satisfy doubters with regard to the question of capital punishment. Maybe the right to life, which is guaranteed in the charter, in some way affects the possibility of restoring or abolishing capital punishment. There are certainly some doubters on that point. I see some hon. members in the backbenches behind the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) nodding in assent.
What about the question of euthanasia? It also affects the right to life. Why do we not say that nothing in this charter prevents us legislating on that? What about genetic engineering? What about all the doubts that will arise on every other subject? We have the right to have conscription, maybe; the right to send men to war to kill other people or be killed themselves. All these things may cause doubt in some people's minds.
This is to say, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot expect in advance, in the short time we have, without the test of the application of this charter in the courts and without some experimentation with its effects, to bring all the doubters home, as the hon. member would like to see us do.
I will go on to another argument which once again affects not particularly this amendment but others. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has handed me several pages of argument to the effect that this amendment is not only unnecessary but could, indeed, be harmful because, by excluding from the charter the right to do something as regards abortion, lawyers and judges might be inclined to conclude that since we made that exclusion for abortion and did not make it for euthanasia, capital punishment and so on, therefore the charter itself precludes the Parliament of Canada from legislating in those areas.
That is just one of the many arguments the Minister of Justice has just handed me. I will not go into them at this stage. They are all good, but it seems to me we have another reason which does not affect only this amendment, but which affects the amendment moved earlier by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and no doubt will affect other amendments which will be moved in the course of today, Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. I want to explain the attitude this party has as regards those amendments.
When I was meeting with the ten provincial first ministers on November 3, 4 and 5 I was meeting them not only with the desire of this party but with that of others to seek one final compromise, which I must say in my own heart I was not very optimistic about reaching, though I was very determined, as was the Minister of Justice who was assisting me, that we would ago as far as was conceivably possible to try to make an accord possible. Not only was that argued on this side of the
November 27, 1981

House, it was a very firm enjoinder of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), who made strong, I would say almost vociferous, statements to the effect that if we went there and did not negotiate in good faith, they would fight us tooth and nail all the way. They would not let us go to London.
I must say this was not surprising coming from the Leader of the Opposition. This has always been his position, and I respect it. But the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who has been a supporter of the previous resolution before the House, made it very clear to me too that if there was not some compromise, if there was not a genuine attempt to reach an agreement, he would not be able to guarantee that he or his caucus would support this party in the resolution which was then before the House.
The Government of Canada went to that meeting of first ministers intent on compromise, intent on reaching agreement even if that meant giving up some parts of the charter or, indeed, some formula for amending which we thought, and, as I indicated in answer to questions earlier today, probably still think, is better than the one with which we are now going to proceed to Westminster. But we compromised. We were asked to compromise and we did compromise.
The result is that we reached an accord which is historic not only in content but in bringing into effect the will of the Canadian people and of successive governments since they began the attempt in 1927, to give a constitution to Canada, the only sovereign country in the world which until now, and it is still true today, did not have its own constitution amendable in its own country-a constitution as a result of an accord which would have these historic, momentous dimensions.
This did mean on this side giving up quite a bit. It meant telling the premiers: We will give in to you when you want a non obstante clause; we will give in to you when you do not want the Victoria formula but prefer the Vancouver formula- which was also the preferred formula of the Leader of the Opposition-but at least we will sign this accord in good faith and will undertake as a government to see it through the House of Commons. I think we have lived up to the spirit of that accord until now.
It is true that with regard to the two amendments, one concerning women and equality between the sexes, and the other concerning aboriginal rights and the entrenchment thereof in the Constitution, the Minister of Justice did support changes. He did so after consulting with the nine signatories to the accord who gave their consent in circumstances which are known.
It is true also that in an effort to reach out to the government of Quebec we also brought in other amendments, one on the Canada clause and the other on some form of compensation when there is opting out of constitutional change in areas concerning culture and language, two subjects which, of course, are very important to the preservation of the identity of the French-speaking Canadians who are largely citizens of Canada residing in Quebec. It is true that the Minister of Justice did this. He did this in the case of the first two
The Constitution
amendments because I think the results showed that if the equality of sexes amendment and the aboriginal rights amendment were left out of the accord, it was not the result of a wilful desire of the ten signatories to take out of it what had been before the House and the country for a year. In that sense I think the Minister of Justice, though I know he felt he was walking on eggs, treading gingerly, knew every time he picked up a phone to speak to the premier or attorney general of a province he was risking their saying: "Look, what are you people doing in Ottawa? You are trying to force us, blackmail us or threaten us into recognizing such and such a pressure from such and such a lobby group. You are end-running the accord." I must say the provinces have shown a great deal of forebearance and the Minister of Justice a great deal of patience in getting the improvements we already have.
I say, as regards the two amendments relating to the particular situation of Quebec, that they were not only brought before the House with the consent of the nine signatory provinces, but with the support, I believe it is fair to say, of at least a majority of the official opposition and of the NDP because they, as we on this side, feel it was and is important to bring the province of Quebec, through its legal government-I say "legal", but is it legitimate; I am not sure-into signing this accord.
That is the story of the amendments we had until now. That is why, from now on, when it comes to improving the charter in ways that had not been put before the House or had not been accepted in the previous resolution, improving the charter to bring doubters home as the present amendment suggests, or improving the charter to give satisfaction to the requests of the Council of the Northwest Territories or Yukon, as the amendment brought in by the member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) does, we say those improvements should be made in the charter when it is in Canada and when we have an amending formula to improve that charter.
I think that was the point of view expressed ad nauseam by the official opposition last year when we were trying to-

we gave them when we signed that accord, that imperfect as it was, we would be bound by that accord and we would not try to make end runs in order to improve it in some way that had not been done through the accord.
Once again, for a year the official opposition has been telling us that it wants a charter written in Canada, that it does not want it to be done in London and does not want Westminster to tell Canadians what their rights are. For the past ten days they have been trying to change this resolution so as to tell Westminster to tell us what this charter should be. Surely a minimum of consistency should be required. We had a charter. We have one now. It is not perfect, nor was it in the previous resolution, but now that we have an accord, now that we are proceeding to Westminster at least in a way in which the courts indicated was not only legal but constitutional, let the accord and the resolution go to Westminster. Let it come back and let us use the amending formula not only to bring other doubters on board if we have to, but even then to continue trying to bring the government of Quebec on side and hopefully as well the government of Ontario when it comes to entrenching Section 133.
These are the tasks ahead of us, Mr. Speaker. We should now turn our efforts in these last days to making sure that we do not destroy the historic accord of November 5. My caucus, my cabinet and I have reached this conclusion in past discussions, including one which we had this morning amongst several ministers in which we said that from now on we cannot risk accepting any amendments, no matter how desirable, because they do risk endangering the accord.
I think the first precept of ethics is to make sure that the aim for the better does not destroy the good.
We had made this decision and I told the leader of the House that I intended to speak in this way on this amendment, but just 15 minutes ago I was handed the text of a telex sent to me by the premier of British Columbia who, as we know, is the chairman of the premiers' conference for this year.
It is a telegram that was not solicited by me or my government and of which I had no knowledge until after we had made the decision that I have just announced.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read this telegram which has reached my office by telephone. I am told the telex is on its way. The telegram reads:
1 am writing to you on behalf of the nine provinces that signed the November 5 constitutional accord. The agreement reached in Ottawa is a significant achievement in the affairs of our nation and was only possible through compromise on the part of all of us. I have been asked by my colleagues to inform you that additional constitutional change should only be considered in Canada following the patriation of our Constitution. My colleagues and I believe that further negotiation must not put at risk the accord and that the package should be approved by Parliament as it now stands and proceeded with without further delay.
That is the position of the nine provinces which signed the accord. That is the position of this government and, regardless of the merits or demerits of any amendment put forth between now and the adoption of this measure, this government, and I hope members of this caucus, will respect the word we gave when we signed that accord and will agree to be bound by a
compromise agreement which was constantly described as the Canadian way, by a compromise agreement which we signed in good faith and which we will defend in this House with utmost vigour.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this House take most seriously the telegram that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has just read. I hope the House will still take the time and the courage to consider some of the amendments that are to come before the House yet, such as the one in relation to the consent of the aboriginal peoples of this country.
I would like to speak to the amendment put before the House by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and to inform him and all members of the House that it is our opinion and that of the Department of Justice that the Constitution is neutral on the issue of abortion, and intentionally so.
Despite this, if what the member says is true, there is definitely a flexible amending formula, of which all members of the House are aware, and also the fact that seven of the consenting provinces are led by premiers of the same party as the hon. member.
I would like to deal for a moment with the last-minute amendment put forward without notice that is now before us. It is something that the Conservative House leader and the member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) took offence to our party doing yesterday when we introduced the consent clause in relation to aboriginal rights. They condemned us for not giving the House time to see the text and to consider it, to perhaps have caucus meetings and an opportunity to prepare speech notes before coming into the House. For that reason it is somewhat regrettable that they have suddenly moved this amendment.
It is the view of our party, Mr. Speaker, that it is clearly a redundant amendment, explicitly so, to use the same words as those used by the hon. member. It is an attempt to inflame the argument on both sides of this issue. For what purpose? I have listened to the Conservatives-the member for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker), the previous House leader of that party, just yesterday, calling for support for the resolution, and he certainly was not alone in that party. It is neither necessary nor appropriate to spell out the proposed amendment in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
There is the danger in the constitutional sense that by specifically preserving Parliament's power in this area, the courts could draw the implication that Parliament's power is somehow diminished in other areas which are not named in
November 27, 1981

just such a clause. This is a very potent argument and one carefully avoided-in fact, perhaps purposely absent-in the argument put forward by the hon. member for Rosedale in the hope of drawing attention away from the issue of constitutional law to one of morality, to various possible court decisions and the very function of this House.
Why is the Conservative Party singling out abortion but not capital punishment, for example, and what is the signal they intend to send out, first to the Canadian public and, more specifically, to the courts? The answer is clear. This is an attempt by the Conservative Party to play the most devious kind of politics, and I say that without intending any slur or touching in any way on the honestly-held beliefs of the hon. member for Rosedale.
Where is the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald)? I know that just a few hours ago she was unaware of this Tory action, this Conservative amendment. She was in Kingston today and is now hoping to get back, and I am confident she would fight against this kind of action taken, no doubt, to rally the Conservative caucus around an idea-a deeply felt issue, I admit, on the broader scale of human life-but it is certainly not specified here or in the amendment or in any of the legal arguments we have heard in the House or in the committee.
It has been made to seem that, through some sleight of hand, this was not previously dealt with in the committee or here in the House. The moral, legal and medical arguments on the issue of abortion are only to be dealt with by Parliament, and always will be. This sleight of hand-this trick-was twice lost this year already and is resurrected-for what reason I can only wonder.
I ask all hon. members of this House to refer to Votes and Proceedings of April 23, 1981, to look at the clause put forward by the Conservative Party at that time and to reflect on the fact that it was lost by a vote of 175 to 93. When this was under very intense scrutiny before the joint House of Commons and Senate committee on January 30 of this year, a very similar clause was put forward. However, it included capital punishment, and it also was sufficiently lost during the committee stage.
Where is the capital punishment part of that clause in this amendment, or is it to be the next amendment of the Conservative Party? And where are the other social questions which could also have serious constitutional and legal implications for the interpretation of the charter? I will deal with capital punishment in a moment.
As I said earlier, this is a redundant amendment. The Conservatives say it is to make explicit what they say is, somehow shadily, implicitly taken away from Parliament. That is a crude political portrayal of months of legal argument on this issue. Even though twice lost, the Conservatives have again sought the spotlight, not to settle this issue as they claim but to ask Canadians perhaps to gaze askance at the charter and to set the mood out there that perhaps some of them are going to vote against the package or against some part of it
The Constitution
and that somehow the Parliament of Canada is giving over something very vital to the courts.
As I have said earlier, if what they say comes true, there will be ways very early in the future to deal with it. This issue is vested, just as is capital punishment, with the House and with the collective moral conscience of all the men and women elected to this place.
The issue of capital punishment is perhaps not here, as it was on both previous votes, because the Conservative leader himself is opposed to it in principle. Also the attempt is to force the issue of abortion in a new way through the courts through the Constitution. I urge all those listening to this debate in the House to see this for what it is. It is not an attempt by members of the official opposition to clarify what they now call a glaring error in the Constitution but a dangerous play to fire up the Canadian public by calling a concern a shadow, a shadow a vagary and a vagary a reality, and thus a constitutional flaw. History will prove me correct that this staged debate is no more than a fabrication.
I have my views on the issue of abortion, and I have stood firmly by those views through two consecutive elections. Many Conservatives have their views as well, but to use this forum and this debate to put forward their views, veiled in the artificial shroud of fact, is a sad way to respond to this issue and to the fabric of this nation.

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should include the follwoing question in the 1981 census:

planned murder?"
He said: Mr. Speaker, I placed this motion on the Order Paper on April 30, 1980, with a view to having it debated prior to the 1981 census. It has just now been called, more than a year and a half later, and the census has already been taken. Whether there is any purpose in debating the motion is questionable, but since it has been ordained by the House that private members' hour must go ahead, I suppose I have no choice.
My view of a representative of the people is that he or she, to the greatest possible degree, should reflect the thinking of the people who sent the member to a legislature or to Parliament. My view of a government is that it should reflect the thinking, to the greatest possible degree, of the majority of the people they endeavour to govern.
This is the premise upon which I endeavour to act as the representative of the people of Bow River. I am sure many other hon. members follow the same premise. If a member feels that way, he or she has a responsibility to find out how his or her people feel about various issues and questions. In my own riding I have no doubt because the matters were discussed very definitely at fora. From knocking on some 8,000 to 10,000 doors, I know that a great majority of the people indicated that they wanted capital punishment for carefully planned murders reinstated. Consequently, that is what I believe I should present to the House of Commons. In addition it is my own conviction.
In order to find out how Canadians feel about this matter, I thought there was no better way than doing it through a consensus where practically every Canadian family is contacted, so that they would have an opportunity to say how they felt
November 27, 1981

in regard to capital punishment. A simple question could have been included on the census paper. It could have read:
Do you favour the reinstatement of capital punishment for deliberately planned murder?
It would not have been difficult for people to answer yes or no to the particular question. However the government did not see fit to bring it forward in time for the 1981 census. All we can do now is discuss the matter after the fact and possibly have the question included on the next census.
We have some indication as to how the people of Canada feel. The Government of Canada does not prepare legislation on the basis of one constituency. It prepares its legislation on the basis of the majority of the population. There are different ways to find out how people feel. It can be through the representations of every Member of Parliament or through Gallup Polls.
[DOT] <mo)
I want to refer briefly to what the people of Canada have said to the government about capital punishment. I do not intend to discuss the merits or demerits of capital punishment to any great degree at this time, but I will endeavour to show that governments should reflect the thinking of the people. The people have spoken very, very clearly. I do not believe in the totalitarian philosophy-that the government knows best; that the government should tell the people how they feel; that the government should tell the people what is good for them. I do not believe in that philosophy at all. I believe that the government should find out what the people at the grassroots think and then reflect that thinking in the laws of the country.
I think every party pays attention to the Gallup poll, so let us examine the polls for the last few years to see what they show is the concerted thinking of the people on this particular topic. The publication "The Gallup Report" of August 6, 1977, begins as follows:
In spite of the fact that Parliament voted to abolish capital punishment last summer, a large proportion of the Canadian electorate still are in favour of this form of punishment.
Today, 75 per cent favour the death sentence for the killing of a prison guard or an on-duty policeman; while almost as many Canadians (74 per cent) would like to see it for murders committed by terrorists. Somewhat fewer, but still a solid majority (68 per cent) favour capital punishment for the killing of any innocent person.
The people of Canada spoke very loudly and told Parliament that they did not support the law that had been passed a few months previously. The report shows that people feel very strongly about the murder of prison guards and policemen. Today, 75 per cent to 80 per cent of people feel that if a prison guard or police officer is killed in the course of duty, the murderer should suffer death as well. The report showed that for the murder of any innocent person, a child or a woman or an elderly man, 68 per cent to 69 per cent of the people felt that capital punishment should be imposed.
On April 19, 1978 "The Gallup Report" began as follows:
When questioned about a recent suggestion that a referendum be held on the issue of capital punishment at the time of the next federal election, over
Capital Punishment
eight-in-ten Canadians said they would favour such a vote; 12 per cent opposed it-
The people had said that the government was passing legislation with which they did not agree and that they wanted to have a way of telling the government how they felt. The following question was posed:
Would you yourself be in favour or opposed to a vote being held on the issue of capital punishment?
The response was 82 per cent in favour of a vote. In effect, the people said that they wanted to tell the government how they felt. The response was broken down into age groups. Many people feel that the young people are opposed to capital punishment but the response showed that in the age group 18 to 29, 80 per cent wanted the right to tell the government how they felt; in the age group 30 to 49, it was 81 per cent and for 50 and over it was 84 per cent. So across the board, more than 80 per cent of the people thought that the government should let them say how they felt about capital punishment for deliberately planned murder.
In 1979 the same question was asked, "Do you favour or oppose capital punishment (a) for the killing of a prison guard or on-duty policemen?" The response was from 70 per cent to 79 per cent in favour. For the killing of any innocent person the response was 68 per cent to 69 per cent in favour of capital punishment. The questionnaire also dealt with terrorists but I will not go into that. In 1979, however, more than 70 per cent of the response favoured the reinstatement of capital punishment for the killing of a police officer or prison guard and almost 70 per cent favoured reinstatement for the deliberate killing of an innocent person.
On March 25, 1981 "The Gallup Report" began as follows:
There has been little change over the past two years in the attitude of Canadians towards the death penalty. Today, 73 per cent favour it for the killing of a prison guard or on-duty policeman; 74 per cent for terrorists; and 67 per cent for the killing of any innocent person.
Let us analyse the results, Mr. Speaker. For the killing of a prison guard or an on-duty policeman the response was 70 per cent to 73 per cent in favour with only 7 per cent not having an opinion; for the killing of any innocent person the response showed that 67 per cent or 68 per cent of people wanted the death penalty brought back for those who kill our little girls, our little boys, our elderly people-sometimes for their own lust and gratification. The people had spoken again in 1981.
Throughout these Gallup polls in which many people place a lot of faith, it has been shown that the people are consistent in asking for the return of capital punishment for the deliberate murder of prison guards, on-duty policemen or any innocent person. Apparently the government will not listen to what the people have to say.
In his householder of January, 1981, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) asked whether constituents favoured the imposition of capital punishment for premeditated first-degree murder. The response showed that 87.2 per cent of those polled asked for the return of the death penalty. The result was broken down into urban and rural categories showing the response of adults and of youths.

November 27, 1981
Capital Punishment
I think the people of Canada have a right to expect that the government will reflect their thinking. More than two thirds of all the polls indicate that the people of Canada want the return of capital punishment.
There was an ideal opportunity to get the opinion of almost every Canadian on this subject had my motion been brought forward prior to the 1981 census. The question "Do you favour the reinstatement of capital punishment for deliberately planned murder?" could have been included in the census form. The response would have given the government an indication of how the vast majority of people in Canada feel about this important subject. The government was not prepared to include that question, however, so we do not have the information. It would have been a more sensible question than asking how many bathtubs are in a house.
A few years ago when I was in provincial politics I conducted a poll through public meetings. After debating both sides of the question results showed that 82 per cent of the people at those meetings, from all political parties, favoured the reinstatement of capital punishment.
Today, crime is running rampant and violent crime is becoming all too prevalent throughout the country. The elderly, and particularly elderly women, are afraid to walk outside after dark in some of our cities. We are more concerned with treating the criminals justly than we are concerned with the victims. The rights of law-abiding citizens seem to be eroding with the increasing leniency toward crime, prison sentences and punishment.
Some people say that we should not worry because those who commit hideous sexual crimes, particularly those against little boys and girls, will be killed by fellow prisoners. That is a great way to have justice! The country should face its own responsibility! When someone commits a crime, such as the one where a little girl was terribly abused and then killed, surely that is deliberate murder and it should not be condoned.
People should not be put into prison for 20 years and then released. There are many cases where people have been in prison once, twice or three times, and they have come out and killed someone else. That is not justice, in my view. It is not the type which gives people a sense of security.
I consider, for example, the heinous crime committed in my own constituency last year. I appreciate the tremendous concern expressed by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan). Perhaps all the cabinet ministers were concerned, and I believe I can say that every hon. member in the House was concerned. That little girl was taken out under there pretext that she was to babysit, and her parents never saw her alive again. Who knows what she went through in those hours before the monster who took her, tied rocks to her and sent her to the bottom of a lake in southern Alberta? He is still running at large. If he is apprehended, there will be the bleeding hearts who will say, "Oh, poor man. He is sick". He was so sick to have planned, deliberated and committed a crime that he does not deserve to live.
It is time we took this type of crime seriously. Sixty six per cent to 90 per cent of the people of Canada cannot be wrong. We are asking the government to take cognizance of and give recognition to what the people of Canada are saying in regard to reinstating capital punishment. Let us show that if criminals murder, deliberately, they have no right to life themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join in this debate because I was one of the Members of Parliament, along with many of my colleagues, who were present in the House at the time this vote was taken. I can recall that for some 18 months prior to the vote, there was not a time when I could go home on the weekends and talk to my constituents or, for that matter, even to people around the Hill, who did not have very strong opinions about capital punishment.
If I could address myself directly to the motion, it is surely out of order in the sense that nothing can be done about the 1981 census. The intent of the motion is to have the people of Canada generally decide whether there should be a return to capital punishment. I question whether this type of query should be answered by way of a census. If this question is put to the people, should we not also have a question on abortion? Should we not also have a question on euthanasia? Should we not also question people on to the use of nuclear power? Surely, if anything were to go wrong there, it would mean the loss of thousands of lives.
I think that once we start putting these questions by way of a census, we must have some kind of an idea as to why we would take a census. Would it be to get opinions from people, or hard facts? Why should we obtain these facts from a census? Surely, it would help us to view the make-up of our country.
If we want to get the opinions of the people of Canada, we can do that through an election. We in the House of Commons are the spokesmen for our regions throughout the country. As we have all been present in the House in these last hours, and as so many people are here listening to our words of wisdom, I would point out that we will probably be influencing everyone who is in the House of Commons. Indeed, if I were simply to
November 27, 1981

influence half the people present and get their agreement, I am sure it would go a long way toward showing the people of Canada just exactly what is thought of the motion which has been raised, and, perhaps what is generally thought of the private members' hour.
However, I wish to address myself in part to the issue of capital punishment itself. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) spoke earlier about Gallup polls and polls which he had taken in his own meetings where people of various political persuasions were present to give their opinions. Perhaps I could share with him and with all my other colleagues in the House the results obtained when I took such a poll. I was the Member of Parliament for St. Catharines at the time.
I prepared and sent out a questionnaire for householders. At the time, there were 40,000 householders in my riding of St. Catharines. It should be kept in mind that this was the most pressing problem for most of the people of Canada, and it was the one issue my constituents wanted to discuss with me on the weekends when I went home. This was the issue which, in its intensity and importance, took up virtually all of the waking time of some people.
I sent out my questionnaire to the people of my former riding so that they could share with me in making this decision. Out of 40,000 questionnaires which were sent out, the grand total of 2,255 people shared with me their perception of capital punishment. It amounted to less than 8 per cent. Only 7.3 per cent of the people who were sent questionnaires took the time to let me know what they were thinking when they had the opportunity to respond to their Member of Parliament.
We could agree, but then say that if we decide on the census, it would force the people to answer. Perhaps it would. Capital punishment was a burning issue at the time 1 sent out the questionnaires. I ask myself and hon. members here, is this the way we should conduct ourselves? Is this the way that such a very important question should be decided, by poll results? Or should we view the question in the quietness and solitude of our own minds and consciences? Can the state take the life of one of its citizens? Do we have the power to play God? Shall we decide who deserves to live and who does not?
I personally believe that the state does have the right to take a human life. The conditions I laid out then have not changed for me. I voted in favour of capital punishment then because long ago, when I was in university, 1 learned in the study of apologetics that for a person to be truly responsible for an act, he must, first of all, know that the act is wrong. I agree with the hon. member. If the man deliberately, wholeheartedly, coolly and methodically plans a murder, he must know it is wrong. First, he must know the deed is wrong. Second, by wanting to commit murder, he has exercised his will, knowing the deed is wrong yet wanting to carry it out. Third, he plans his crime over a long period of time. I can hear the question, how long is the period of time. I say, long enough for someone to plan a sequence of events leading to such a hideous crime. Finally, the crime must be committed. There are four steps. Those are the four conditions which, as said, if they exist, then that individual who knowingly, wilfully, methodically, carried
Capital Punishment
out a murder whether against a young girl, a young boy or an older person, it does not matter, against another human being, has forfeited his right to live in this society. After proving beyond any shadow of a doubt that this crime was planned, perpetrated and finally committed, after due process of the law and recourse to the courts of appeal and after all the demands for mercy have run out, I believe now as I did before that the state has the right to take a human life.
I have looked at other facts aside from recognizing the logic of this conclusion. Many times I have heard that the lives of murderers should be taken because they will kill again. But what are the facts to support that? From the time that England abolished capital punishment until January 1975 we know that 308 men and women were tried and convicted of first degree murder. To wilfully plan and commit murder carries the ultimate charge of murder in the first degree.
But these 308 men and women in England convicted of First degree murder evidently were not hanged. They were not put to death. How many of them committed murder again? If 300 of them committed murder a second time, then we must conclude that they should have been put to death. If 200 of them committed murder a second time, then we should conclude that because over 50 per cent committed murder a second time, they should be put to death. And if only ten committed murder a second time out of a total of 308, then 298 did not do it a second time.
From the figures I quoted at the time I spoke on capital punishment and declared my stand on the issue, of the 308 men and women who had been convicted of murder in England up to January, 1975, one, and only one, committed murder again. Yet 307 other men and women would have been put to death as well. What happened to them? I do not have the case histories of them in front of me. I know that a number of them, I think of three in particular, who were convicted of murder wrote books giving us an insight into their lives before the crime and into their lives in prison. I know that these people, who are not among us now, experienced a great change in their lives.
I am not for one moment saying that we were right to give them a second chance, but I am saying there might be a doubt in our minds about these people who commit heinous crimes that they are beyond redemption in the sense that they are beyond doing any good for society.
Since voting on this issue, I have had a great deal of time for second thoughts. The other day the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), when he was asked a question in this House as to whether capital punishment would again be considered, quoted a figure which surprised me. He said that the number of murders committed in Canada had declined on a year-to-year basis since the abolition of capital punishment. What do we conclude from that? Do we conclude that the action we took in abolishing capital punishment has convinced more people not to commit murder? I do not know.

November 27, 1981
Capital Punishment

I wish I had the answer to all those questions. Mr. Speaker, when, for some reason or other, men and women take away the life of one of their fellow citizens, we really have no idea what was going on in their mind when they committed their crime. We must ask ourselves whether or not, in some way or other, it may not be that society, the type of life they led, programmed them to commit their crime. Four or five months ago, I met five men all members of the same family. Thank heavens, none of them had committed murder. Yet, the five brothers were in prison at the same time. One must wonder why they were in jail, all at the same time. Could it be because of their home life? Because of the environment in which they grew up, perhaps the school they attended? What motivated them? If only we had the time, perhaps we could change the situations which lead people to commit this or that crime.

If I can return to the question itself, Mr. Speaker. The motion put forward by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is simple. He asks that the question be included in a census. I have asked myself, I have questioned the hon. member for Bow River as well as my colleagues, whether this is the way to go about getting the information we seek. I wish I had a nice easy answer and I wish I could say to the hon. member that he is dead wrong. I wish I could say to him that he should not suggest seeking the answer that way. But if I say that, then I have to come up with a better way to glean the answer. I do not know if it is a better way in the sense that we will get a real answer, but I think the system we have devised for members such as ourselves is to get as much information as we can. But more than that, we should get all the information we can through reading and by listening to the debates here, then after struggling with our consciences, decide, each one of us individually, if the state does have a right to take a life. Perhaps then we would come to a decision which would be best for the individual concerned, ourselves as legislators and, indeed, the citizens of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to repeat that the motion we are debating once again brings capital punishment to the attention of hon. members. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should include the following question in the 1981 Census:
"Do you favour the reinstatement of capital punishment for deliberately planned murder?"
As the previous speaker has pointed out, the question really is out of order because obviously the 1981 census has been taken. I found that the question was put on the Order Paper in April, 1980. Perhaps the next time it would behoove the hon. member for Bow River to put in a clause to cover the possibility of a similar situation arising, because if his motion is dated, there is a chance it will be irrelevant. Nevertheless, I think the hon. member has made some points and put forward some issues which deserve consideration.
I sense in my constituency a growing concern that there is more emphasis being placed on the rehabilitation of an individual who has done physical damage to another individual than on the victim, in some cases a victim who has lost his life. There is no amount of rehabilitation, psychiatric treatment, pill or anything that can return a life. I sense in my constituency the feeling that in society as a whole we have lost this balance.
I should like to address this problem as I feel there are two major areas in which we can improve the situation. First, there should be better methods of protection for the general population from those who have already shown, by their deeds, that they are capable of physical harm to another person. I would give as an example the individual who has committed rape upon a child, or some other horrendous deed, and where it has been shown there is an associated mental disorder.
Unless evidence is produced through the medical community, or that community which deals with criminology, that this pattern of behaviour can be changed, and no such evidence has been produced, then I think it is incumbent upon those who make the laws in our country, that is hon. members here and in the legislatures, to ensure that such individuals not be allowed back into society. The reason I say that is the probability that such an individual will commit the same kind of crime. We know there is no cure for the mental condition exhibited by the individual who commits the kind of crime I have just described. We know that no amount of rehabilitation can eradicate that kind of behaviour on the part of an individual who has demonstrated the ability to commit that kind of crime, the rape of a small child and murder. I have referred to that example because that was the example given by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I feel society has the right to be protected from this type of individual when it has been established that there is a mental disorder which allows the commission of such violent acts.
It is time we made our views strongly known to the provincial governments which have the responsibility of enforcing existing legislation, such as the Criminal Code. Unfortunately many people feel the federal government is the enforcer of such legislation. In point of fact, the responsibility for the enforcement of the law in most criminal areas lies with provincial governments and those judges who handle most of these criminal cases.
Let me refer again to this matter of protection. A previous speaker suggested that the number of murders had decreased since the removal of capital punishment. I think we have to look with some suspicion at that statistic. I have discussed this issue with judges and lawyers in my area. I have learned that the number of murders shown by the statistics is not the same as the number of murders actually committed. First of all, there is the matter of charges being reduced from murder to manslaughter and, secondly, there are the not-obvious murders. An example would be the individual who decides to murder someone and then commit suicide by getting into a car and hitting another car head-on. There is a whole spectrum of murder from those that are not obvious through to the cold-
November 27, 1981

hearted, deliberate murder described by the previous speaker. It is quite difficult to use statistics in relation to murder to come to any conclusion about capital punishment.
What we really want to do is to establish in Canada a social milieu in which we have as few murders as possible. How can we do that? This brings me to the second major area I want to discuss, and that is the area of prevention. I think one thing we can do in order to achieve this goal is to stress the importance and value of human life and its first priority over anything else in our society. We can talk about this, but the fact is that in many little ways, which mount up to a big way, we put material things far ahead of respect for and value of human life. This involves a challenge not just for politicians, educators, teachers, professors and those engaged in business and labour, but for all Canadians, the challenge to reassess their values. Human life is at the apex.
The last point I would like to make on this issue is that I am concerned. I do not think it is idle talk to be speaking of the value of human life at this time. I believe that at this time in history it is one of the most important subjects we should be talking about.
The value of human life must become a political issue, especially when I hear the President of the United States talking about the feasibility of a limited nuclear war involving the deaths of 100 million people or talking about the feasibility of pressing the button first to start a nuclear war. I hear of military strategists saying they may lose 100 million people in a war but they will win it because it is worth it. This is an issue which people should consider when electing their leaders.
